Chapter Two: Challenging Authority and the Birth of a Movement
Picture this—the world beyond the monastery walls is shifting fast. Thanks to the printing press, new ideas are flying from town to town, and people everywhere are starting to question the old ways. Have you ever felt frustrated by a system that seems unfair? That’s exactly how many folks felt about the church’s sale of indulgences—these little certificates that promised forgiveness if you just paid up. For some, buying one brought peace of mind. But for others, it was like a flashing warning sign that something was seriously off.
Martin—by now a respected professor and preacher—can’t shake his discomfort. Day after day, he watches regular people, desperate for hope, spending their hard-earned money on indulgences. They believe it’ll guarantee their place in heaven. Church leaders insist it’s all perfectly fine, claiming tradition and scripture are on their side. But Martin? He just can’t square it with what he’s found in the Bible. There’s a gap between the church’s message and what the gospel really says.
One day, Martin reaches his breaking point. He decides he just can’t stay silent anymore. So he writes down ninety-five points—questions and criticisms about selling indulgences. Then, in a move that would change history, he posts them right on the church door in Wittenberg. Back then, that was how you invited a good, old-fashioned debate among scholars. Martin never expects what happens next. His document gets copied, printed, and suddenly, it’s everywhere across Germany. In a heartbeat, Martin finds himself in the eye of a storm.
People from every walk of life get caught up in the debate. Some see Martin as a hero, finally standing up to corruption and fighting for the true faith. Others think he’s a troublemaker, threatening both the church and the peace of society. Church leaders demand he take it all back, but Martin stands his ground. He says his conscience is tied to the word of God, and he just can’t go against what he believes is right.
Things only heat up from here. Martin’s called on to defend his views before church officials. The pressure? It’s intense. And the risks? They’re huge—challenging the church could mean excommunication, prison, or worse. But Martin doesn’t budge. He keeps insisting that faith should be rooted in scripture, not just in traditions or the decisions of popes and councils.
As the controversy grows, Martin’s ideas break out of the university and spread far and wide. Suddenly, everyday people—many of whom never dared question the church before—start to imagine real change. What began as a single act of protest turns into something so much bigger: a movement for reform that will shake the very foundations of European society.
Through it all, Martin stays a reluctant leader—a man fueled not by dreams of fame or power, but by a deep sense of responsibility to speak the truth as he sees it. The cost is steep: friendships fall apart, alliances crumble, and danger is never far from his door. Still, Martin’s willingness to stand alone, to risk everything for his conscience, lights a fire in others to do the same.
These years are a blur of faith and authority, of tradition battling with reform. The church, once the unshakable heart of spiritual life, becomes the center of fierce debate. And for so many, the real question shifts. It’s no longer just, “Should things change?” but rather, “What kind of change—and who gets to decide?”
